families.s: HSE general workplace electrical-hazard and precaution guidance
families.t: shock, burns, arcing, fire, explosion, robust equipment, isolation, maintenance, competence and emergency switching
f: Electricity can kill or severely injure people and can damage property.
Main electrical hazards include electric shock, burns, arcing, fire and explosion.
Cables, plugs, sockets and fittings should be robust enough and protected for the working environment.
Machinery should have an accessible switch or isolator so power can be cut off quickly in an emergency.
Electrical equipment and installations must be maintained to prevent danger so far as reasonably practicable.
Damaged plugs, taped or exposed cables, burn marks and overheating signs require equipment to be removed from use.
Electrical repairs should be carried out only by people with the necessary skills, knowledge and experience.
Work planning should identify electrical wires, equipment and buried or overhead services before the task starts.
families.g: Electrical risk depends on voltage, fault energy, environment, equipment condition, earthing and protection, isolation, task, competence and exposure time.

families.s: HSE safe selection and use of electrically powered work equipment
families.t: risk assessment, task suitability, supply compatibility, condition, RCDs, damp or conductive environments, explosive atmospheres, training and PPE
f: Employers should assess the hazards and controls before electrically powered equipment is used.
Equipment should be physically suitable for the task and for the way it will be used.
Equipment condition, plugs, cables and connectors should be checked and damaged equipment removed from service.
Equipment must be compatible with the voltage, current and characteristics of the electrical supply.
An RCD can provide additional protection in appropriate circumstances but does not replace basic electrical safety.
Damp, conductive or restricted spaces may require reduced-voltage, battery, air-powered or other additional precautions.
Equipment for a potentially explosive atmosphere must be selected for that hazardous location.
Users need suitable training and must understand any required PPE and controls.
families.g: Powered-equipment risk depends on task, voltage, supply, environment, wetness, explosive atmosphere, equipment damage, protection devices, user competence and maintenance.

families.s: HSE planning, secure isolation and competence guidance for electrical work
families.t: planning, secure isolation, release of stored energy, decontamination, access, standards, testing and competent work
f: Electrical work should be thoroughly planned so it can be completed safely.
Equipment and installations should be prepared for work by isolating electrical and other energy sources.
Isolation should be secure so energy cannot be inadvertently reintroduced.
Stored mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic or other energy may also need to be released or restrained.
Decontamination or a safe working platform may be required before the electrical task begins.
Installed equipment should be suitable for the task and the environment in which it will operate.
Where practicable, work near wiring or equipment should be done with the supply turned off and controlled against reconnection.
Specialist electrical work requires competence matched to the system, voltage, equipment and hazards.
families.g: Electrical-work risk depends on system design, voltage, stored energy, isolation points, verification, access, environment, work method, competence and restoration controls.

families.s: HSE overhead-power-line planning and proximity-control guidance
families.t: line identification, flashover, avoidance, de-energisation, access controls, goalposts, plant height, routes and line-owner coordination
f: Accidental contact with overhead power lines kills people and causes serious injuries.
Touching a live conductor is not necessary because close approach can cause flashover.
High or long plant such as cranes, MEWPs, tippers, ladders and scaffold poles presents particular risk.
Work near overhead lines must be planned and managed even when the task is short.
The line owner should be consulted so diversion, de-energisation or other precautions can be considered.
Overhead lines should be assumed live unless their owner confirms otherwise.
Safety measures combine planning, eliminating danger, controlling access and controlling the work.
Routes and work zones should prevent plant, loads and people entering unsafe line-clearance distances.
families.g: Overhead-line risk depends on voltage, line height and sag, plant geometry, load movement, weather, ground, access route, line status, supervision and operator competence.

families.s: HSE underground-cable location and safe-excavation guidance
families.t: service plans, locating devices, marking, trial holes, safe digging, insulated tools, repeated scans, emergency work and competence
f: Damaging an underground electrical cable can cause fatal shock, arcing, explosion and severe burns.
Excavation planning should use service plans, locating devices and recognised safe-digging practices.
Plans indicate possible service locations but do not precisely prove a cable's position.
A trained competent person should trace, identify and clearly mark underground services before digging.
Locators should be checked, maintained and used repeatedly as excavation progresses.
Trial holes and careful hand digging may be required to confirm the service route.
Excavation should proceed alongside a service and expose it horizontally where practicable.
Emergency excavation without reliable plans should proceed on the assumption that live buried services are present.
families.g: Underground-cable risk depends on service records, cable depth and route, locator performance, soil and surface, digging method, plant, cable condition, competence and work control.
